extracted.intended_audience: general news readers interested in media and political humor
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and public reaction criteria for assessing political satire (online images/posts) — what makes a satirical image perceived as funny, irresponsible, or offensive. Focuses on use of beloved characters, graphic violence, execution quality, and responsiveness to political context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor should reveal a truth
rubrics_metrics.description: "At the heart of humor is a revealed truth" (quoted from Elon Musk).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good satire should expose or illuminate a truth or insight about its target; without that revealed truth it risks being "humorless." The page contrasts revealed-truth humor with mere shock or ideology-driven mockery (e.g., "woke is a lie, so it is humorless").

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gratuitous or graphic violence for shock value
rubrics_metrics.description: Many users called The Onion's image depicting Goofy "covered in blood" holding a "blood-soaked crowbar" and the post was described as "jarringly unfunny," "gross," and mean-spirited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using explicit gore or depictions of murder as the primary device can provoke disgust rather than laughter and be judged irresponsible; satire that relies mainly on gruesome imagery risks alienating its audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of political climate and responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics labeled the post "irresponsible in today’s political climate," arguing that provocative imagery can have harmful effects given current tensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creators should consider potential real-world consequences and whether a piece escalates division; what might be dismissed as satire in calmer times may now be read as inflammatory or reckless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate asymmetrical backlash and perceived double standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple commentators noted that "if conservatives had made an image with a character murdering a Democrat leader, they would be canceled," highlighting perceived partisan double standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satirists should anticipate differential public and media responses depending on the target and be prepared for accusations of hypocrisy or uneven enforcement of norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid weaponizing beloved children's characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The piece used a "classic character Goofy" in a depiction of murdering a political figure, which many found especially jarring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using iconic or child-associated characters in graphic political violence tends to amplify offense; creators should weigh whether invoking such figures is necessary or gratuitous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production and execution quality affect credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The article notes the image was "poorly photoshopped," implying sloppy execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low-quality visual or textual execution can undermine satirical intent and make a post seem careless or malicious rather than insightful; good craft (clear concept and competent execution) helps convey purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone: avoid being merely mean-spirited or provocative
rubrics_metrics.description: Observers described the post as "mean-spirited" and "not funny," suggesting the satire lacked constructive or witty critique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire that feels purely vindictive or intended to wound rather than illuminate risks reputational damage and audience rejection; aim for wit or insight rather than gratuitous nastiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit, sensational headlines amplify reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: The headline spelled out the violent act: "Goofy Beats Ron DeSantis To Death With Crowbar."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highly explicit or sensational headlines can intensify backlash and broaden visibility (and condemnation); headline wording should be chosen with awareness of how it frames the piece and escalates responses.
